suppression.headline: In oxygen-enriched atmospheres (>22 % O2) a burning droplet went out on its own in 33 % of tests with nitrogen only (n=6), but in 79 % with CO2 in the atmosphere (n=19) and 75 % with helium (n=4).
caveats: Liquid fuel droplets in microgravity, not fabrics or plastics.
Small groups (see n) — read as evidence, not as a guarantee.
FLEX set the suppressant fraction before ignition; it did not test discharging an agent onto a fire.

gas_model_card.scope: Ethane / propane / butane flames on a spherical burner in microgravity.

misconceptions.claim: A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off.
misconceptions.verdict: NASA: research in ground-based laboratories and microgravity experiments 'demonstrates the fallacy of these assumptions' (Researcher's Guide, p. 35).

source.name: NASA Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science (2015), p. 35

misconceptions.claim: A steady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment.
misconceptions.verdict: NASA: research in ground-based laboratories and microgravity experiments 'demonstrates the fallacy of these assumptions' (Researcher's Guide, p. 35).

source.name: NASA Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science (2015), p. 35

misconceptions.claim: Because the reduced-gravity environment is inherently safer, terrestrial fire standards and tests represent a very conservative approach to fire safety.
misconceptions.verdict: NASA: research in ground-based laboratories and microgravity experiments 'demonstrates the fallacy of these assumptions' (Researcher's Guide, p. 35).

source.name: NASA Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science (2015), p. 35

misconceptions.claim: Since many fire detectors operate by sensing fire-generated particulates, they would need to use different signatures to detect fires in microgravity.
misconceptions.verdict: NASA: microgravity research 'highlighted the vastly different particulate size associated with flames in microgravity' (Researcher's Guide, p. 35); see SAME / SAME-R (PSI-102, PSI-101).

source.name: NASA Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science (2015), p. 35

micro.label: Microgravity (ISS, transit)
micro.statement: All PSI flight tests ran in microgravity - predictions below apply here.

earth.label: Earth gravity (1 g)
earth.statement: PSI holds 1 g results only as the ground comparison in Saffire-II (9 samples). The ML models are trained on microgravity tests and are not valid at 1 g.

lunar.label: Moon (1/6 g)
lunar.statement: No partial-gravity combustion data exists in PSI, so no prediction is made. 0 g and 1 g results may not bound this case: microgravity flame spread peaks at low flow speeds (Olson & Ferkul's 'Goldilocks' zone, PSI-62), the kind of weak buoyant flow lunar gravity produces.

mars.label: Mars (3/8 g)
mars.statement: No partial-gravity combustion data exists in PSI, so no prediction is made. 0 g and 1 g results may not bound this case (see the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone, PSI-62).

disclaimer: Research decision support built from NASA PSI experiment data. It is not a crew procedure: real spacecraft fire response follows the vehicle's own flight rules and trained procedures.
